subject: To bin or not to bin, that is the questions

messages.author: e5841ce9d01eda50
messages.subject: To bin or not to bin, that is the questions
parts:
Hello all,

I am using Distance sampling to analyze chimpanzee nests counts and I am not sure if, or how, I should bin my data.
My observation range from 0-70m from the line, but I appear to be violating the assumption of decreasing detectability as you move away from 0.
My observations increase from 0-10m, and then decrease from there. So, does it make sense to bin my data in order to reconcile this?

By binning my data does seem to help the model because when when I truncate the data at the same point, my AIC score does drop from 2,500 (not-binnned) to 1,000 (binned). but I worry about losing too much information or manipulating my data inappropriately.

Thoughts?

If binning is a good option, then my issue is where. If I bin at intervals of 10m, then the first two bars in my histogram area actually flat (not increasing or decreasing), and I end up with 7 bin classes.
Or, I bin my data by 11m intervals so that I have the typical decreasing trend of observation moving away from 0, but I end up with only 6 bin classes.

Is binning my data an appropriate why of remedying my delimna? And if so, how should I make my bin classes so that I'm losing as little information as possible.

Thank you very much to anyone who can offer some insight on this issue!

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: {Disarmed} Re: [distance-sampling] To bin or not to bin, that is the questions
parts:
Adrienne

I'm not an expert on detecting chimpanzee nests, I'm guessing they are in trees.  I suggest it might be more difficult to detect nests when viewed from underneath than when viewed more from the side.

If you analyse the data as exact distances (as the data were collected), using a model with a shoulder such as the half normal, then you may  have a detection function shape that compensates for the nests missed close to the transect: it will miss the first histogram bar high and perhaps fit well for the remaining detections.  But your goodness of fit metrics may suggest poor fit.

You can choose to bin your data for the purpose of fitting a detection function.  However the choice of bins is subjective--there are no guidelines for how to do this.  In particular, using AIC comparisons for different binning choices or truncation distances is invalid, because AIC comparisons are only valid when exactly the same data are fitted to models.  There is also no mandate that all bins are of the same width.  I suspect a complete analysis of the data will likely truncate detections beyond, say 50m as those detections have little information about the shape of the detection function near the transect.

As you can see, there are many types of decisions associated with your questions, but little in the way of objective procedures to assist you. I'm willing to look at your histogram if you wish to send it to me off-list.


Eric Rexstad

messages.subject: {Disarmed} RE: [distance-sampling] To bin or not to bin, that is the questions
parts:
Adrienne, just adding to what Eric has said, you can’t use AIC to compare binned and unbinned analyses – the AIC values are not comparable. 

 

I guess another possible cause of a lack of detected nests near the transect is if the transect tends to avoid trees that might hold nests, for example, if it follows a road or track.  You could consider left-truncating your data, but if you’re detecting roughly the same number of nests between 0 and 10m as between 10 and 20m, I doubt whether it will make much difference.

 

Steve Buckland

Thank you Eric and Steve for your comments. They have been helpful

I'm not really sure why the slight spike in observations after 10m has occurred, other than some kind of observer bias.
My survey and the transects followed a randomized survey design and thus did not follow any trails or roads.
And while nest detection directly above the transect can be an issue and potentially cause a skew in some habitat types it doesn't seem to be a consistent issue across all surveys and in all habitat types.

Looking more closely at the data, the most observations ARE at 0m, and then it decreases, but then spikes again after 10m.

Should I worry about violating an assumption of the analysis?

messages.subject: Re: {Disarmed} RE: {Disarmed} Re: {Disarmed} RE: [distance-sampling] To bin or not to bin, that is the questions
parts:
I decided to not bin the data and analysis it with the exact distances and only modifying by truncation.
The hazard-rate function without adjustments gave me the best AIC score, which, when then tested for goodness of fit gave me a p-value = 0.32
By not binning I was able to retain more information, and while the flatter shoulder at the beginning does miss those slight spikes just after 10m (my original concern), the detection function otherwise appears to fit the data quite well.

Overall, I'm happy with the analysis and certainly feel more confident in the result. Thank you Eric and Steve for your assistance on this issue!

Adrienne
